result.title: UX Best Practices: A Research Brief
result.summary: A grounded synthesis of UX practice across research, architecture, interaction, heuristics, flows, and navigation, drawn from Nielsen Norman Group, Don Norman, Material Design, and observed industry patterns. The brief favors evidence-based methods, established mental models, and measurable outcomes over novelty. Use it as a checklist when designing, reviewing, or auditing digital products.
key_principles: User-centered design: every decision is validated against real user behavior, goals, and contexts, not assumptions.
Progressive disclosure: reveal complexity only as users need it, keeping primary paths fast and shallow.
Consistency and standards: reuse established patterns, terminology, and locations so users transfer prior knowledge across the product.
do_list: Test with at least five real users per iteration and act on observed friction, not stated preferences.
Map user flows end-to-end before designing screens; ensure each flow has a clear entry, success state, and recovery path.
Establish an information hierarchy with one primary action per view and group secondary actions deliberately.
dont_list: Do not hide primary actions behind gestures (long-press, edge swipes) without an equivalent discoverable affordance.
Do not introduce custom iconography that diverges from platform or web conventions without labels and onboarding.
Do not redesign familiar patterns (back button, breadcrumbs, form fields) without a measurable benefit that justifies the relearning cost.

patterns.name: Progressive Disclosure
patterns.description: Show only the essential controls or information up front; surface advanced options on demand via expanders, modals, or secondary panels.
patterns.example: Gmail's 'Compose' reveals a minimal form first and adds Cc/Bcc, formatting, and attachments only when requested.
patterns.use_when: A view serves both novice and expert users, or contains high-density controls that would overwhelm primary users.

patterns.name: Card-Based Layouts
patterns.description: Group related content into discrete, scannable units with consistent structure, visual rhythm, and clear hierarchy.
patterns.example: Linear's inbox groups issues as cards with priority, status, and assignees, enabling rapid triage.
patterns.use_when: Users browse heterogeneous items where each item carries multiple attributes (title, meta, action).

patterns.name: Sticky Primary Navigation
patterns.description: Keep the main navigation or top action persistently visible while content scrolls.
patterns.example: Notion's left sidebar and editor top bar remain fixed so users never lose orientation in long documents.
patterns.use_when: Apps with deep hierarchies, frequent section switching, or long-form content where orientation loss is a risk.

patterns.name: Inline Validation
patterns.description: Validate form fields as users complete them rather than only on submit, with specific, actionable error messages.
patterns.example: Stripe Checkout validates card numbers and expiry in place and shows the exact failing field on submit.
patterns.use_when: Forms with multiple fields, fast-fail inputs (credit cards, emails), or any flow where submit-time errors cause abandonment.

metrics.name: Task Success Rate
metrics.why: Direct measure of whether users can complete primary goals; the single most important UX outcome metric.

metrics.name: Time on Task
metrics.why: Captures efficiency; large increases signal friction or confusion even when success rate is acceptable.

metrics.name: System Usability Scale (SUS)
metrics.why: Validated, comparable cross-product score for perceived usability across sessions and cohorts.

metrics.name: Error Rate
metrics.why: Errors reveal points of misalignment between user mental model and system behavior.

examples.takeaway: Power-user patterns adopted as the default; every action is reachable in 1–2 keystrokes without sacrificing discoverability.

examples.feature: Progressive disclosure in API documentation with code examples first, explanations expandable
examples.takeaway: Lead with the working example; defer theory until users have a working artifact, reducing time-to-first-success.

examples.feature: Slash command menu and block-based editing
examples.takeaway: Contextual commands appear exactly where the user's cursor is, eliminating mode-switching and menus hunting.

examples.feature: Pull-to-refresh and swipe gestures with visible labels
examples.takeaway: Gestures are reinforced by visible affordances and labels during onboarding, avoiding the 'hidden interaction' trap.

references.title: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design

action_items: Run a 5-user moderated usability test on the top three user flows within the next two weeks and prioritize fixes by severity of observed friction.
Audit current navigation against platform conventions (iOS HIG, Material 3, Web Standards) and produce a one-page consistency report.
Measure baseline SUS score for the product and re-measure after each major release to track perceived usability over time.
